## Decision: build this. Promoting from design placeholder to planned work.

Decided on platform direction rather than held for a user request. Sibling issue #3862 was closed as not planned in the same review — the two are not symmetric, and the contrast is the argument for this one.

### Why this is a capability gap, not a nice-to-have

A node returning `{ success: false }` kills the entire run. The only recovery is flow-level `errorHandling.strategy: 'retry'`, which re-runs from the start — useless for a deterministic failure, and wrong for a transient one that only affects a single step.

That means ObjectStack cannot express the most ordinary sentence in business automation:

> If the external API call fails, notify the owner and continue.

Every workflow engine we are compared against can. A record that a `get_record` does not find, an `http` node that 404s, a `connector_action` that rate-limits — these are normal business conditions, not faults, and today each one destroys the whole run. This is table stakes, and it is missing.

### Why it matters more the more guards we add

The platform's main defense against silently-wrong data operations is the family of nodes that refuse to execute: #3810 (filter lost a condition), #3425 (readonly write is a certain no-op), ADR-0049/#1888 (unscoped scheduled run). We are going to keep adding them, because they work.

But each one makes "the guard fired" and "the automation stopped" the same event. That coupling is what the strictness debate on #3810 was actually about — the objection was never that the guard judged wrong, it was that aborting is expensive. This issue decouples them, which means we can keep tightening guards without the cost compounding.

### Hard design constraint (new — this is the part that makes it safe)

**A guard refusal must NOT be routable. Only genuine runtime errors are catchable.**

| Class | Example | Routable? |
|---|---|---|
| The world did not cooperate | `http` 404, no rows matched, connector rate-limited, timeout | **yes** |
| The metadata is wrong | filter lost a condition (#3810), readonly write (#3425), unscoped run (#1888) | **no — stays fatal** |

Without this split, error branches become a strictly worse version of the `$optional` idea just rejected in #3862: an AI author attaches an error edge to every CRUD node and every guard on the platform is silently swallowed. With the split, the guards keep their absoluteness and error branches serve only what they should.

This is also why this issue survives the AI-authoring objection that killed #3862. An error branch **forces the author to write the target node** — it must state what happens instead, and the result is visible in the flow graph. That is an order of magnitude more work than adding a suppressing keyword, and it is reviewable. `$optional` was a silent one-token bypass; this is a drawn edge.

### Scoped v1 (ship this, defer the rest)

- `type: 'error'` on an edge — follows the `type: 'back'` precedent (ADR-0044), where edge type already drives traversal semantics.
- The failing node's message lands in `{<nodeId>.error}` so the branch can act on it.
- **Only runtime errors route.** Guard refusals bypass error edges and stay fatal, per the table above. This needs a distinguishable failure class on the node result, not just a string.
- **Unhandled failures stay fatal**, unchanged. Strict opt-in.
- **Run history must not report a clean success.** A run that took an error branch and completed needs the failure visible on the step — the #3356/#3407 lesson, where a silent 3ms `success` hid a write that never landed.

Deferred out of v1, tracked here:

- Interaction with `errorHandling.retry` (does a handled node still count toward flow-level retry? presumably not).
- Error edges that loop back — needs the same `type: 'back'` cycle treatment or `registerFlow` rejects legitimate retry shapes.
- Whether `label: 'error'` should be accepted as an alias (leaning no — one spelling).

### Sequencing note

Landing this lowers the cost of every guard already shipped and every one we add next, so it should come **before** the next batch of refuse-to-execute guardrails rather than after.

## v1 landed in #3881 — with a correction to this issue's premise

This issue was filed to **build** node-level error branches. On opening the engine, they were already there and working: `type: 'fault'` is in the edge schema, `executeNode` routes both the thrown and returned failure paths to a handler, `$error` is populated, and there were tests. **The feature was never the gap.**

The gap was the hard constraint added when this was promoted — and it was live in `main`:

> **A guard refusal must NOT be routable. Only genuine runtime errors are catchable.**

`fault` edges routed **everything**, guards included. Reproduced before fixing: a `fault` edge on a `delete_record` whose filter carries a typo (`{record.ownr}`) made #3810's protection against emptying the object disappear — the guard fired, the handler swallowed it, and the run reported `success: true`. One declared edge, and the platform's data-safety guarantee was off.

So the work was a containment fix, not a feature build. Shipped:

- **`NodeExecutionResult.errorClass`** — `'runtime'` (default, so every existing executor keeps its routing) or `'guard'`. Guard-class failures are never routed; they stay fatal with or without a fault edge and fail with the guard's own message.
- **Thrown guards contained too.** `resolveNodeFilter` returns its refusal, `UnscopedRunDataAccessError` throws one; both are covered via a shared `guard-refusal` module. Otherwise the catch path would have become the bypass the return path no longer was.
- **`{<nodeId>.error}`** alongside run-wide `{$error}`, so a handler shared by two fault edges can tell which node it is handling.
- **Run history** was already correct and is now pinned by a test: a run that recovers reports success, and the failed step keeps `status: 'failure'` with its message.
- **Documentation** — fault edges were entirely undocumented. Added to `content/docs/automation/flows.mdx` and the automation skill, including the routable/not-routable table and an explicit instruction not to add a fault edge to silence a guard error.

407 tests pass in `service-automation` with no regressions; the pre-existing fault-edge tests still pass, which is what defaulting to `runtime` is for.

### Still open here

- Interaction with flow-level `errorHandling.retry` — does a handled node still count toward flow-level retry? (Presumably not.)
- Error edges that loop back — needs the ADR-0044 `type: 'back'` cycle treatment, or `registerFlow` rejects legitimate retry shapes.
- Whether `label: 'error'` should be an accepted alias (leaning no — one spelling).

Leaving this open for those three. The safety property and the v1 ergonomics are done.

Findings triage round (triage seat Routine, 2026-08-07): **hold — but the restart condition is rewritten, because the old one could not be exited.**

The 08-06 01:15Z grading ended with "等 services 车道有 appetite 时由发现分诊轮晋级或按倾向逐项收口关闭". "When the lane has appetite" is not a condition anybody can evaluate — it is the exact shape SKILL bans (*a hold without a restart condition is a state nobody can ever legally exit*). This round measured all three v2 residuals against `origin/main` (`1eb13a0`) instead, and two of the three turn out to be already settled.

## Residual-by-residual status (measured, not recalled)

**③ `label: 'error'` alias — settled, will not be done. Closing this residual.**
Zero occurrences of a `label`-based error alias in `service-automation/src` or `packages/spec/src`. Better than absence: `content/docs/automation/flows.mdx:869` states the rule positively — "**`type: 'fault'` is what routes — a label is not**" — and `content/docs/releases/v17.mdx:1365` lists "`label: 'error'` written where `type: 'fault'` was meant" as a *named author error*. The recorded 倾向 (不做) is now the documented, shipped position. Adding the alias would contradict published release notes. ⛔ Do not reopen this one without a maintainer ruling.

**② error-edge loop-back — the open question is answered, and the answer is sharper than the question.**
`engine.ts:4108-4112` (`detectCycles`) builds its adjacency list from **every** edge and skips only `type === 'back'`. A fault edge that closes a cycle is therefore included in the DAG analysis and rejected by `registerFlow`. So the original phrasing ("error 边回环需 `type:'back'` 同款环校验") is answered: it already gets the same validation.

The real residual is what the rejection tells the author to do. `flow.zod.ts:440` declares `type: z.enum(['default','fault','conditional','back'])` — **single-valued, so `fault` and `back` are mutually exclusive.** The error message at `engine.ts:4145` says *"mark the cycle-closing edge with `type: 'back'` (ADR-0044)"*, and following it converts the edge from a fault edge into an ordinary back edge — **silently discarding the error-routing semantic the author wanted.** A looping fault edge is currently inexpressible, and the prescribed remedy destroys the intent rather than refusing it.

Direction matters here and it is the good one: this is **fail-closed** (`registerFlow` throws; nothing runs). No guard is bypassed, no run silently swallows a failure. That is why this stays a finding rather than becoming queue work.

**① does a handled node count toward flow-level `errorHandling.retry` — genuinely still open.**
No linkage between fault-handled nodes and retry accounting exists in `service-automation/src` (`retry`/`attempt` hits are all flow-level: `engine.ts:4986`, `flow-retry-attempt-count.test.ts`, `try-catch-node.ts:75`). The recorded 倾向 ("不计,因为失败已被处理") remains un-implemented and un-contradicted. Unlike ② and ③, this one still needs a decision before it needs code.

## New restart condition (replaces "when the lane has appetite")

Promote to `pm:queue` when **any one** of these is true — each is mechanically checkable:

1. **A flow author is first observed wanting a looping fault edge** (a `registerFlow` rejection where the intended edge was `type: 'fault'` closing a cycle). That turns ② from inexpressible-in-theory into a blocked user, and it is the point at which the `fault`/`back` exclusivity needs a real answer (a `back`+fault composition, or an explicit refusal message that says the loop is unsupported rather than suggesting a lossy substitute).
2. **Residual ① becomes reachable** — i.e. a flow ships with both a fault edge and `errorHandling.strategy: 'retry'`, making "does the handled node count" an answer the engine must actually give. Today the combination is untested and the ambiguity is invisible.
3. **Anyone opens `engine.ts` `detectCycles` or the `errorHandling` retry accounting for another reason** — the ② message fix is a few lines and should ride along rather than occupy its own claim.

If none of the three has fired by the time the services lane next runs a findings sweep, ⛔ do not re-grade this from scratch: residuals ② and ③ are closed above, so only ① is live, and ① is a decision card (`needs-user-decision`), not queue work — escalate it rather than dispatching it.

## Stale-premise note on this issue's body

Already recorded in the 07-28 14:15Z comment, restated because it is easy to lose: **the body's premise is dead.** Fault edges were never the gap — they existed and worked; #3881 shipped the containment fix (`errorClass: 'runtime' | 'guard'`, guard refusals never routable, `{<nodeId>.error}`, run-history pin, docs). Verified still in place this round: `guard-refusal.ts` (4 hits), `engine.ts` (2), `guard-refusal-inventory.test.ts` (2). Anyone reading only the title and body will try to build a feature that exists.

## Spun out of this check

Filed **#6094** (`pm:queue`, `domain:spec`): the `fallbackNodeId` tombstone at `flow.zod.ts:715` prescribes `condition: 'fault'` where the routing slot is `type` — i.e. the spec's own migration message hands authors a variant of the very error `flows.mdx:869` and `v17.mdx:1365` warn about. Found while confirming residual ③. It is a separate one-line spec fix, deliberately **not** folded into this issue — this one is a services-lane design residual, that one is a `domain:spec` string.
